screens.title: Control Structures and Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on the core building blocks that control program flow inside smart contracts. You will learn how to make conditional decisions with if and else, how to repeat actions using for and while loops, and how to stop execution intentionally using require, revert, and assert. We’ll also introduce custom errors as a gas-efficient way to report problems and revisit safety considerations such as unbounded loops, integer bounds, and a brief introduction to reentrancy. These ideas matter because control flow determines correctness, gas cost, and security. For example, a misplaced loop can exhaust gas and block a payout function, while a missing require can allow unauthorized state changes. Through short code examples and a hands-on voting contract, you’ll see how to validate inputs, guard access, and choose the right error mechanism. As you follow the examples, ask yourself: which conditions are external inputs and which are internal invariants? That distinction guides whether to use require, revert, or assert and helps you design safer contracts.

Control Structures and Error Handling
Decide, iterate, and fail intentionally to build secure, predictable smart contracts.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this first objectives panel we break the chapter into actionable skills you can verify. First, you will implement conditional logic with if and else in Solidity, which matters because access control and input validation depend on clear branch choices. For example, only the owner should be allowed to change a protected value; implementing that check prevents unauthorized state changes. Second, you will use for loops to iterate over small, bounded arrays. A practical use is summing scores or processing a fixed small list, but you must always weigh gas cost. Third, you will apply require and revert to enforce preconditions and report errors to callers; using these correctly refunds gas and provides meaningful messages. Fourth, you will reserve assert for internal invariants that should never fail, a choice that signals catastrophic bugs when triggered. Each skill is measurable: write a function with an if/else guard, add a bounded for loop, replace an if-fail with require or revert, and include one assert for an invariant. These objectives help you write clearer, safer contracts.

screens.title: If / Else: Conditional Logic in Solidity
screens.narratorSegment: Conditionals let a contract change behavior based on inputs or internal state. In Solidity, an if statement evaluates a boolean expression and executes code when that expression is true; else captures the alternate path. This is how access control is often implemented: check whether the caller is the owner, then allow a state change. A concrete example is a function that sets a value only if the caller equals the stored owner. If the condition fails, you should handle it explicitly with an error rather than silently doing nothing. A common misconception is that silent failures are acceptable; they leave callers unsure whether a transaction succeeded and can hide bugs. When you need multiple disjoint checks, use if, else if, and else to return descriptive strings or values depending on ranges. In practice, combine conditionals with require or revert to provide clear failure semantics and a gas refund. As a reflective question, consider which conditions are external inputs and which are internal invariants, because that determines whether you validate with require or assert. If / Else: Conditional Logic in Solidity means use conditionals to enforce business logic and pair them with explicit errors so callers know why a transaction reverted.. In practical terms, use boolean checks to guard actions and return status. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › If / Else
Definition
Conditional branching
Evaluate booleans to choose execution paths, often used for access checks and state-based responses.
Example: only owner can set value using if-check plus an explicit revert if unauthorized.
Common mistake: silently failing when a condition is false. Prefer explicit errors.
Key Takeaway

Always pair conditional decisions with clear failure behavior so callers understand outcomes and gas is handled predictably.

Code Example
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract ConditionalExample {
    uint256 public value;
    address public owner;

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
        value = 100;
    }

    function setValue(uint256 _newValue) public {
        if (msg.sender == owner) {
            value = _newValue;
        } else {
            // prefer explicit errors like require or revert instead of silent failure
            revert("Caller is not the owner");
        }
    }
}
Pro tip: prefer require for simple preconditions.
Check your assumptions: who can call this function?

screens.title: Chained Conditionals and Return Values
screens.narratorSegment: Chained conditionals let you express multiple branches cleanly, returning different results depending on ranges or state. A typical pattern is checking value ranges to return a status string, for example returning 'Value is high', 'Value is medium', or 'Value is low' depending on thresholds. This is useful for on-chain view functions that summarize contract state or for gating different fee tiers. A misconception to avoid is overusing long string messages within require or revert when compact custom errors could be more efficient; for readable view functions, returning strings is fine, but for revert reasons prefer concise messages or custom errors. Another practical consideration: chain checks from most specific to most general to avoid unintended matches. Always consider gas: view functions that return strings are read-only and do not cost gas when called off-chain, but on-chain string ops can be expensive if included in state changes. To deepen understanding, try converting a chain of if/else if/else branches into compact early returns and compare readability. Chained Conditionals and Return Values means order checks from specific to general, and choose return strings for views but concise errors for reverts.. In practical terms, use if, else if, else for multi-way decisions and status messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Chained Conditionals
Pattern
Multi-way decisions
Use else if to test descending thresholds so only one branch runs and outcomes are predictable.
Example: return status text from a view function based on numeric ranges.
Misconception: Strings in require are costly in storage; prefer compact errors when reverting state.
Check your understanding

Why would you test the highest threshold first rather than the lowest? Think about matching precedence.

Code
function checkValueStatus() public view returns (string memory) {
    if (value > 200) {
        return "Value is high";
    } else if (value > 100) {
        return "Value is medium";
    } else {
        return "Value is low";
    }
}
Pro tip: keep thresholds clear and document units.
Real example: fee tiers based on numeric thresholds use the same structure.

screens.title: For Loops: Iteration and Gas
screens.narratorSegment: For loops are the primary iteration tool in Solidity for processing arrays or repeating fixed work. A typical pattern uses a counter variable that increments until it reaches a length. For example, initializing an array in a constructor with a small fixed number of entries is safe and common. However, each loop iteration consumes gas, and the total gas cost increases linearly with the number of iterations. If the array can grow without bound, a for loop that always iterates over every element can eventually exceed the block gas limit and cause the transaction to revert. This is a real vulnerability because it can turn into a denial-of-service where functions that rely on iterating become unusable. A practical mitigation is to design contract interactions so that no single transaction must iterate over a large dynamic collection. Use pull payments, let users claim individually, or process items in small batches under explicit limits. Also consider saving intermediate progress off-chain and resuming with bounded loops. The key point is to use for loops, but only under predictable, bounded conditions. For Loops: Iteration and Gas means every loop iteration costs gas; avoid unbounded loops and prefer pull or batch approaches for large collections.. In practical terms, iterate over arrays carefully; gas cost grows with each iteration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › For Loops & Gas
Pattern
Bounded iteration
Use for loops for small fixed-size collections or batch processing with explicit limits to control gas usage.
Example: constructor populates a small array with five numbers using a for loop.
Warning: iterating over a dynamic, growing array in one transaction risks hitting the block gas limit.
Real-world connection

When writing payouts or mass updates, design for users to pull funds or employ paginated batches to avoid failures as collections grow.

Code Example
uint256[] public numbers;

constructor() {
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        numbers.push(i + 1); // numbers will be [1,2,3,4,5]
    }
}

function sumNumbers() public view returns (uint256 total) {
    total = 0;
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {
        total += numbers[i];
    }
}
Pro tip: cap lengths or require limits for on-chain loops.
Alternative: use events to record items and process them off-chain.

screens.title: While Loops and Their Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: While loops repeat work while a condition remains true and are less common in Solidity for array iteration. A simple use case is a pure function that decrements a counter until zero, useful for algorithmic calculations that do not modify state. The reason they are less common is the same as for unbounded for loops: unless you can guarantee the loop completes quickly, you risk consuming excessive gas and reverting the transaction. A concrete example is a countdown that returns zero; this is safe when the start value is small or when the function is pure and used off-chain for computation. A common mistake is using while to process an unbounded collection with external calls — that is a high-risk pattern. Prefer deterministic for loops with known bounds for arrays, and prefer off-chain processing or batching for variable workloads. Ask yourself: can this work be done by participants in parallel or pulled later? If yes, move it off the main transaction path. While Loops and Their Use Cases means use while for small, predictable computations; avoid it for unbounded or external-call work to prevent gas exhaustion.. In practical terms, when while is appropriate and why for is often preferred. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › While Loops
Use Case
Deterministic pure computations
While loops can implement countdowns or algorithmic steps when the iteration count is predictable and small.
Example: a pure function that decrements a counter until zero and returns the result.
Misuse: never drive a while loop with a dynamic user list or external calls that could grow unbounded.
Code
function countdown(uint256 start) public pure returns (uint256) {
    uint256 current = start;
    while (current > 0) {
        current--;
        // pure calculation, safe when start is small
    }
    return current; // will return 0
}
Pro tip

Prefer while for off-chain computations or small pure functions; avoid on-chain loops with unpredictable length.

screens.title: Error Handling: require, revert, assert
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity provides three primary primitives for stopping execution: require, revert, and assert. Require and revert are for external-facing checks and input validation. If a require condition fails, execution stops, state changes roll back, and remaining gas is refunded to the caller; you can provide an error message string to explain why. Revert behaves similarly and is useful inside conditional blocks where the single-line require syntax is insufficient. Assert is different: it checks internal invariants that should never fail. If assert triggers, it consumes all remaining gas and signals a serious contract bug or corrupted state. The practical rule of thumb is to use require or revert for user inputs and preconditions, and to reserve assert for conditions that indicate a fault in your own logic. A common misconception is using assert for input validation — that makes failures appear catastrophic and wastes gas. A concrete example: check that only the owner can call a setter with require, use revert when more complex branching is needed, and use assert to ensure your invariants hold after state updates. Which condition is internal and which is external determines the right tool.

keyIdea.text: Use require/revert for input and precondition checks, assert only for internal invariants that should never be false.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › require / revert / assert
Comparison Table
require(condition, message): validate inputs, refunds remaining gas when false.
revert(message): explicit failure inside logic branches; also refunds remaining gas.
assert(condition): internal invariant checks; consumes all remaining gas when false.
Common mistake

Do not use assert to validate user-provided inputs. Use require or revert so callers get refunds and messages.

Example
function setValue(uint256 _newValue) public {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Caller is not the owner");
    require(_newValue <= 1000, "New value exceeds maximum limit of 1000");
    value = _newValue;
}

function criticalInvariantCheck() public view {
    assert(value >= 0); // internal invariant for demonstration
}
Pro tip: error messages improve developer UX when debugging.
Audit note: assert failures should be rare and signal urgent fixes.

screens.title: Refactoring with require and revert
screens.narratorSegment: A common improvement is to replace silent branch fallthroughs with explicit require or revert checks. This makes failures visible and refunds remaining gas to callers. Consider a setter that earlier used an if to check ownership and did nothing otherwise. That silent behavior leaves the caller uncertain and could hide bugs. Refactor by asserting ownership with require at the start of the function, and validate inputs with additional require statements. If a more complex path requires conditional logic, use revert inside the else branch with a concise message or a custom error to save gas. Always prefer fail-fast checks so state changes do not occur under invalid conditions. The code example on screen shows two require checks: one for ownership and one for an upper bound on the new value. Someone testing the function in Remix will see clear revert messages in the console which aids debugging. After making this change, test expected and failing paths to confirm both behavior and gas refund semantics. In practical terms, turn silent failure into explicit, gas-refunding checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Refactor with require
Before vs After
Before: silent failure branch. After: explicit require checks at function start and revert for branch-specific errors. This clarifies intent and helps callers recover.
Practice: replace any conditional that silently ignores bad callers with require or revert to expose failure reasons.
Check

After adding requires, run successful and failing transactions to observe revert messages and gas refund behavior in Remix.

Refactored code
function setValue(uint256 _newValue) public {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Caller is not the owner");
    require(_newValue <= 1000, "New value exceeds maximum limit of 1000");
    value = _newValue;
}

function withdrawFunds(uint256 _amount) public {
    if (_amount == 0) {
        revert("Withdrawal amount must be greater than zero");
    }
    // withdrawal logic here
}
Pro tip: short messages are fine; use custom errors later for gas savings.
Test: ensure revert messages appear in failed transactions so you can debug quickly.

screens.title: Custom Errors: Gas-efficient Reverts
screens.narratorSegment: Custom errors, introduced in Solidity 0.8.4 and later, let you declare error types and revert with those types instead of long string messages. This is more gas-efficient because strings are expensive to store and return on revert. Custom errors can include typed parameters, making them richer and still cheaper than concatenated strings. A concrete example is defining NotOwner or InvalidAmount with parameters such as provided and required values. When you revert using a custom error, tools and logs can surface the error type and parameters, improving debuggability. A common misconception is that custom errors are only for large projects; in fact, any contract that expects frequent reverts benefits from lower gas costs and clearer failure signals. Use custom errors when you care about gas efficiency on revert paths and when you want structured, typed failure information that tooling can parse. Remember that custom errors require a compatible compiler version and that you should still design clear preconditions to minimize revert frequency. Custom Errors: Gas-efficient Reverts means custom errors save gas and provide typed failure data; prefer them for contracts with frequent or parameterized reverts.. In practical terms, define typed errors to reduce gas and provide structured context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Custom Errors
Why use custom errors?
Gas efficiency and structure
Custom errors let you revert with typed, parameterized error types rather than long strings, saving gas.
Example: error InvalidAmount(uint256 provided, uint256 required) gives precise context with lower gas cost.
Compiler note

Custom errors require Solidity 0.8.4 or newer. They are best used where revert messages are frequent or parameterized.

Code
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.4;

contract CustomErrorExample {
    address public owner;

    error NotOwner();
    error InvalidAmount(uint256 provided, uint256 required);

    constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }

    function doSomethingOnlyOwnerCan(uint256 _amount) public {
        if (msg.sender != owner) revert NotOwner();
        if (_amount == 0) revert InvalidAmount({provided: _amount, required: 1});
        // logic
    }
}
Pro tip: custom errors make logs easier to parse in indexers and testing frameworks.

screens.title: Unbounded Loops and DoS Risk
screens.narratorSegment: Unbounded loops are one of Solidity's most common pitfalls. If a function iterates over a collection that can grow without bound, the iteration cost grows and may eventually exceed the block gas limit. When that happens, any transaction calling that function will always revert, effectively denying service to all users who rely on it. Consider a payout function that loops over registered users and transfers funds: as the list grows, the gas cost for that loop increases until the function is permanently unusable. The practical mitigation is to avoid designing single transactions that must process entire dynamic sets. Instead, implement pull payments where each user claims their funds, or provide a batched processing mechanism that limits the number of items per call. Another approach is to maintain auxiliary structures that cap iteration sizes or use off-chain helpers and events to coordinate multistep processing. The core insight is to design for growth and to remember that gas limits are an operational reality of the network. Unbounded Loops and DoS Risk means avoid on-chain operations that require iterating over potentially large collections in a single transaction; prefer pull or batched patterns.. In practical terms, why growing arrays can break contract functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Unbounded Loops
Risk
Denial-of-Service by gas exhaustion
A loop over a dynamically growing collection may eventually require more gas than allowed per block, causing permanent reverts.
Mitigation: pull payments let each user claim funds separately.
Mitigation: batch processing with explicit limits to control per-transaction work.
Example Scenario
A function that distributes rewards by iterating the entire registeredUsers array works fine at small scale but fails as the array grows. A safer design is to let users call claimReward(), or provide an owner-driven batched process that handles N users per call.
Check: when you design a loop, estimate worst-case gas and ensure it stays below block limits or use an alternative pattern.

screens.title: Integer Bounds and unchecked Blocks
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding integer overflow and underflow is essential for safe arithmetic. Since Solidity 0.8.0, arithmetic operations revert automatically on overflow or underflow, which prevents many classic mistakes. That behavior makes code safer by default, but developers must remain aware of any use of unchecked blocks, which disable automatic checks for performance or gas reasons. Using unchecked can reintroduce overflow risks if you do not reason carefully about bounds. A concrete example is summing values into a counter; if the counter could theoretically wrap, reliance on automatic checks is appropriate. A common misconception is that modern compilers make overflow impossible; in fact, unchecked disables the guard and shifts responsibility to the developer. For legacy code or libraries that intentionally use unchecked arithmetic, document and constrain inputs rigidly and consider unit tests that exercise boundary conditions. The safety-first approach is to prefer the default checked arithmetic unless a measured performance need justifies unchecked. Integer Bounds and unchecked Blocks means solidity 0.8+ reverts on overflow by default; only use unchecked when you can prove bounds and need the gas savings.. In practical terms, how solidity 0.8+ handles overflow and when to use unchecked. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Behavior
Automatic checks in modern Solidity
Solidity 0.8+ reverts on overflow and underflow. This prevents many common errors automatically.
Use default checked arithmetic unless you need micro-optimized loops.
If using unchecked blocks, document why and add tests for boundary values.
Practical check
For counters, balances, and critical arithmetic, prefer checked operations. Only profile and then opt into unchecked when you can prove it’s safe and beneficial.
Quiz question: Why would an unchecked block be dangerous in a token transfer function? Consider wrap-around risk if amounts are attacker-controlled.

screens.title: Reentrancy: What It Is and the Primary Defense
screens.narratorSegment: Reentrancy occurs when a contract makes an external call and the called contract calls back into the original contract before the original call completes. This can be exploited to perform repeated operations, for example draining funds before balances are updated. The primary defense pattern is Checks-Effects-Interactions: first validate inputs and preconditions, then update internal state, and only then interact with external contracts. By updating state before making external calls you remove the window an attacker needs to reenter against inconsistent state. A practical misconception is thinking that transfer or send are always safe; while these forward limited gas and can help, they are not foolproof. Also, use reentrancy guards for added protection and be cautious when calling unknown code. For this chapter we introduce the concept; deeper mitigation strategies, formal proofs, and patterns such as pull payments and reentrancy mutexes will be examined later. As a reflective question, examine every external call in your code: does it occur after state updates? Reentrancy: What It Is and the Primary Defense means always perform checks and state updates before interacting with external contracts to minimize reentrancy windows.. In practical terms, understand recursive external calls and the checks-effects-interactions pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Threat
External calls can enable recursive entry
If you make an external call before updating state, a malicious callee can re-enter and exploit inconsistent state.
Defense: Checks-Effects-Interactions — check inputs, mutate state, then interact.
Supplement: add reentrancy guards and prefer pull patterns for value transfers.
Practical prompt
Review any function that transfers Ether or calls external contracts. Can an attacker call back into the contract before its state is updated? If yes, refactor using Checks-Effects-Interactions.
Note: we'll revisit reentrancy in depth later; for now, treat external calls as high-risk operations.

screens.title: VotingContract Walkthrough (Remix)
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through implementing and testing a simple VotingContract in Remix. The contract stores candidate names, vote counts, and whether an address has voted. Key defensive measures used in the example include require checks for voting uniqueness and candidate validity, custom errors for owner-only functions, and a for loop to compute totals that is safe only because the number of candidates is small. To practice, create VotingContract. sol in Remix, compile with Solidity 0.8. x or higher and supply a small array of candidate names on deploy. Try addCandidate as the owner and verify that non-owners trigger the NotOwner custom error. Vote from multiple accounts to see that hasVoted prevents double voting and that invalid candidate IDs revert. Finally, call getTotalVotes which sums votes in a for loop; note that this is acceptable for a small candidate list but would need redesign for a large dynamic set. This activity reinforces require, revert, custom errors, and the practical gas considerations around loops. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › VotingContract Lab
Activity Objective
Build and test a voting contract
Implement require checks, use custom errors for owner-only actions, and test small-loop totals in Remix using several accounts.
Guided steps: create file, paste code, compile, deploy with a small list of candidates, test both success and revert paths.
Observation: note revert messages vs custom errors in the console during failed transactions.
Try this

As an exercise, add a require to the addCandidate function to cap maximum candidates and observe how that prevents unbounded loops.

Starter code (paste into Remix)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract VotingContract {
    address public owner;
    string[] public candidateNames;
    mapping(uint256 => uint256) public votes; // candidateId => voteCount
    mapping(address => bool) public hasVoted;

    error NotOwner();
    error AlreadyVoted();
    error InvalidCandidateId();

    constructor(string[] memory _candidateNames) {
        owner = msg.sender;
        require(_candidateNames.length > 0, "Must provide at least one candidate.");
        candidateNames = _candidateNames;
    }

    function addCandidate(string memory _name) public {
        if (msg.sender != owner) revert NotOwner();
        candidateNames.push(_name);
    }

    function vote(uint256 _candidateId) public {
        require(!hasVoted[msg.sender], "You have already voted.");
        require(_candidateId < candidateNames.length, "Invalid candidate ID.");

        votes[_candidateId]++;
        hasVoted[msg.sender] = true;
    }

    function getTotalVotes() public view returns (uint256) {
        uint256 total = 0;
        for (uint256 i = 0; i < candidateNames.length; i++) {
            total += votes[i];
        }
        return total;
    }
}
Note: Deploy with a small candidate array like ["Alice","Bob","Charlie"] to keep loops safe during testing.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essentials to carry forward. First, use conditionals to enforce behavior and pair them with explicit errors so outcomes are clear; prefer require and revert for input validation and reserve assert for internal invariants. Second, loops are powerful but costly: ensure loops are bounded or implement pull and batch patterns to avoid denial-of-service through gas exhaustion. Third, custom errors provide gas-efficient, typed reverts and are a better alternative to long string messages when reverts are expected. Keep these three ideas at the center of your design: validate early, limit on-chain work, and communicate failures efficiently. As you write contracts, ask whether each loop is bounded, whether each external call happens after state updates, and whether a revert message should be a string or a custom error. These checks will reduce bugs and surface problems earlier in testing and production.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.narratorSegment: A short reference to carry into your coding sessions: First, always fail fast with require or revert for invalid inputs so state is never mutated under bad conditions. Second, avoid on-chain work that scales with unbounded datasets; instead use pull payments, batching, or off-chain coordination. Third, prefer custom errors for frequent revert paths to reduce gas and provide typed diagnostic data. Keep these rules in mind as you implement conditional logic, loops, and error reporting; they will make your contracts easier to test, cheaper to use, and more resilient to common attacks. As you code, ask: can a loop grow arbitrarily, and does each external call happen after state updates? If you can answer yes to both checks, you’re designing with safety in mind. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on the core building blocks that control program flow inside smart contracts. You will learn how to make conditional decisions with if and else, how to repeat actions using for and while loops, and how to stop execution intentionally using require, revert, and assert. We’ll also introduce custom errors as a gas-efficient way to report problems and revisit safety considerations such as unbounded loops, integer bounds, and a brief introduction to reentrancy. These ideas matter because control flow determines correctness, gas cost, and security. For example, a misplaced loop can exhaust gas and block a payout function, while a missing require can allow unauthorized state changes. Through short code examples and a hands-on voting contract, you’ll see how to validate inputs, guard access, and choose the right error mechanism. As you follow the examples, ask yourself: which conditions are external inputs and which are internal invariants? That distinction guides whether to use require, revert, or assert and helps you design safer contracts.

In this first objectives panel we break the chapter into actionable skills you can verify. First, you will implement conditional logic with if and else in Solidity, which matters because access control and input validation depend on clear branch choices. For example, only the owner should be allowed to change a protected value; implementing that check prevents unauthorized state changes. Second, you will use for loops to iterate over small, bounded arrays. A practical use is summing scores or processing a fixed small list, but you must always weigh gas cost. Third, you will apply require and revert to enforce preconditions and report errors to callers; using these correctly refunds gas and provides meaningful messages. Fourth, you will reserve assert for internal invariants that should never fail, a choice that signals catastrophic bugs when triggered. Each skill is measurable: write a function with an if/else guard, add a bounded for loop, replace an if-fail with require or revert, and include one assert for an invariant. These objectives help you write clearer, safer contracts.

This second objectives panel expands on error types, custom errors, and security considerations. First, you will implement custom errors to make reverts more gas-efficient and expressive. A practical example is defining a NotOwner error and reverting with it instead of a long string message. Second, you will understand integer overflow and underflow risks, and why Solidity versions 0.8 and later revert automatically — but you must still be aware when using unchecked blocks. Third, you will identify unbounded loops as a denial-of-service risk and learn design patterns such as pull payments or batching to mitigate it. Fourth, you will get a conceptual introduction to reentrancy and the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern to reduce risk when making external calls. Each card maps to a measurable outcome: define a custom error, explain automatic overflow behavior, refactor a payout pattern to pull payments, and describe Checks-Effects-Interactions in your own words. Together these objectives build defensive, gas-aware contract code.

Conditionals let a contract change behavior based on inputs or internal state. In Solidity, an if statement evaluates a boolean expression and executes code when that expression is true; else captures the alternate path. This is how access control is often implemented: check whether the caller is the owner, then allow a state change. A concrete example is a function that sets a value only if the caller equals the stored owner. If the condition fails, you should handle it explicitly with an error rather than silently doing nothing. A common misconception is that silent failures are acceptable; they leave callers unsure whether a transaction succeeded and can hide bugs. When you need multiple disjoint checks, use if, else if, and else to return descriptive strings or values depending on ranges. In practice, combine conditionals with require or revert to provide clear failure semantics and a gas refund. As a reflective question, consider which conditions are external inputs and which are internal invariants, because that determines whether you validate with require or assert. If / Else: Conditional Logic in Solidity means use conditionals to enforce business logic and pair them with explicit errors so callers know why a transaction reverted.. In practical terms, use boolean checks to guard actions and return status. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Chained conditionals let you express multiple branches cleanly, returning different results depending on ranges or state. A typical pattern is checking value ranges to return a status string, for example returning 'Value is high', 'Value is medium', or 'Value is low' depending on thresholds. This is useful for on-chain view functions that summarize contract state or for gating different fee tiers. A misconception to avoid is overusing long string messages within require or revert when compact custom errors could be more efficient; for readable view functions, returning strings is fine, but for revert reasons prefer concise messages or custom errors. Another practical consideration: chain checks from most specific to most general to avoid unintended matches. Always consider gas: view functions that return strings are read-only and do not cost gas when called off-chain, but on-chain string ops can be expensive if included in state changes. To deepen understanding, try converting a chain of if/else if/else branches into compact early returns and compare readability. Chained Conditionals and Return Values means order checks from specific to general, and choose return strings for views but concise errors for reverts.. In practical terms, use if, else if, else for multi-way decisions and status messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

For loops are the primary iteration tool in Solidity for processing arrays or repeating fixed work. A typical pattern uses a counter variable that increments until it reaches a length. For example, initializing an array in a constructor with a small fixed number of entries is safe and common. However, each loop iteration consumes gas, and the total gas cost increases linearly with the number of iterations. If the array can grow without bound, a for loop that always iterates over every element can eventually exceed the block gas limit and cause the transaction to revert. This is a real vulnerability because it can turn into a denial-of-service where functions that rely on iterating become unusable. A practical mitigation is to design contract interactions so that no single transaction must iterate over a large dynamic collection. Use pull payments, let users claim individually, or process items in small batches under explicit limits. Also consider saving intermediate progress off-chain and resuming with bounded loops. The key point is to use for loops, but only under predictable, bounded conditions. For Loops: Iteration and Gas means every loop iteration costs gas; avoid unbounded loops and prefer pull or batch approaches for large collections.. In practical terms, iterate over arrays carefully; gas cost grows with each iteration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

While loops repeat work while a condition remains true and are less common in Solidity for array iteration. A simple use case is a pure function that decrements a counter until zero, useful for algorithmic calculations that do not modify state. The reason they are less common is the same as for unbounded for loops: unless you can guarantee the loop completes quickly, you risk consuming excessive gas and reverting the transaction. Solidity provides three primary primitives for stopping execution: require, revert, and assert. Require and revert are for external-facing checks and input validation. If a require condition fails, execution stops, state changes roll back, and remaining gas is refunded to the caller; you can provide an error message string to explain why. Revert behaves similarly and is useful inside conditional blocks where the single-line require syntax is insufficient. Assert is different: it checks internal invariants that should never fail. If assert triggers, it consumes all remaining gas and signals a serious contract bug or corrupted state. The practical rule of thumb is to use require or revert for user inputs and preconditions, and to reserve assert for conditions that indicate a fault in your own logic. A common misconception is using assert for input validation — that makes failures appear catastrophic and wastes gas. A concrete example: check that only the owner can call a setter with require, use revert when more complex branching is needed, and use assert to ensure your invariants hold after state updates. Which condition is internal and which is external determines the right tool.

A common improvement is to replace silent branch fallthroughs with explicit require or revert checks. This makes failures visible and refunds remaining gas to callers. Consider a setter that earlier used an if to check ownership and did nothing otherwise. That silent behavior leaves the caller uncertain and could hide bugs. Refactor by asserting ownership with require at the start of the function, and validate inputs with additional require statements. If a more complex path requires conditional logic, use revert inside the else branch with a concise message or a custom error to save gas. Always prefer fail-fast checks so state changes do not occur under invalid conditions. Custom errors, introduced in Solidity 0.8.4 and later, let you declare error types and revert with those types instead of long string messages. This is more gas-efficient because strings are expensive to store and return on revert. Custom errors can include typed parameters, making them richer and still cheaper than concatenated strings. A concrete example is defining NotOwner or InvalidAmount with parameters such as provided and required values. When you revert using a custom error, tools and logs can surface the error type and parameters, improving debuggability. A common misconception is that custom errors are only for large projects; in fact, any contract that expects frequent reverts benefits from lower gas costs and clearer failure signals. Use custom errors when you care about gas efficiency on revert paths and when you want structured, typed failure information that tooling can parse. Remember that custom errors require a compatible compiler version and that you should still design clear preconditions to minimize revert frequency. Unbounded loops are one of Solidity's most common pitfalls. If a function iterates over a collection that can grow without bound, the iteration cost grows and may eventually exceed the block gas limit. When that happens, any transaction calling that function will always revert, effectively denying service to all users who rely on it. Consider a payout function that loops over registered users and transfers funds: as the list grows, the gas cost for that loop increases until the function is permanently unusable. The practical mitigation is to avoid designing single transactions that must process entire dynamic sets. Instead, implement pull payments where each user claims their funds, or provide a batched processing mechanism that limits the number of items per call. Another approach is to maintain auxiliary structures that cap iteration sizes or use off-chain helpers and events to coordinate multistep processing. The core insight is to design for growth and to remember that gas limits are an operational reality of the network. Unbounded Loops and DoS Risk means avoid on-chain operations that require iterating over potentially large collections in a single transaction; prefer pull or batched patterns.. Understanding integer overflow and underflow is essential for safe arithmetic. Since Solidity 0.8.0, arithmetic operations revert automatically on overflow or underflow, which prevents many classic mistakes. That behavior makes code safer by default, but developers must remain aware of any use of unchecked blocks, which disable automatic checks for performance or gas reasons. Using unchecked can reintroduce overflow risks if you do not reason carefully about bounds. A concrete example is summing values into a counter; if the counter could theoretically wrap, reliance on automatic checks is appropriate. A common misconception is that modern compilers make overflow impossible; in fact, unchecked disables the guard and shifts responsibility to the developer. For legacy code or libraries that intentionally use unchecked arithmetic, document and constrain inputs rigidly and consider unit tests that exercise boundary conditions. The safety-first approach is to prefer the default checked arithmetic unless a measured performance need justifies unchecked. Reentrancy occurs when a contract makes an external call and the called contract calls back into the original contract before the original call completes. This can be exploited to perform repeated operations, for example draining funds before balances are updated. The primary defense pattern is Checks-Effects-Interactions: first validate inputs and preconditions, then update internal state, and only then interact with external contracts. By updating state before making external calls you remove the window an attacker needs to reenter against inconsistent state. A practical misconception is thinking that transfer or send are always safe; while these forward limited gas and can help, they are not foolproof. Also, use reentrancy guards for added protection and be cautious when calling unknown code. For this chapter we introduce the concept; deeper mitigation strategies, formal proofs, and patterns such as pull payments and reentrancy mutexes will be examined later. As a reflective question, examine every external call in your code: does it occur after state updates? Let's summarize the essentials to carry forward. First, use conditionals to enforce behavior and pair them with explicit errors so outcomes are clear; prefer require and revert for input validation and reserve assert for internal invariants. Second, loops are powerful but costly: ensure loops are bounded or implement pull and batch patterns to avoid denial-of-service through gas exhaustion. Third, custom errors provide gas-efficient, typed reverts and are a better alternative to long string messages when reverts are expected. Keep these three ideas at the center of your design: validate early, limit on-chain work, and communicate failures efficiently. As you write contracts, ask whether each loop is bounded, whether each external call happens after state updates, and whether a revert message should be a string or a custom error. These checks will reduce bugs and surface problems earlier in testing and production.

A short reference to carry into your coding sessions: First, always fail fast with require or revert for invalid inputs so state is never mutated under bad conditions. Second, avoid on-chain work that scales with unbounded datasets; instead use pull payments, batching, or off-chain coordination. Third, prefer custom errors for frequent revert paths to reduce gas and provide typed diagnostic data. Keep these rules in mind as you implement conditional logic, loops, and error reporting; they will make your contracts easier to test, cheaper to use, and more resilient to common attacks. As you code, ask: can a loop grow arbitrarily, and does each external call happen after state updates? If you can answer yes to both checks, you’re designing with safety in mind.
